[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [607 U.S. ___](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1287_4gcj.pdf){.cite} [Decided February 20, 2026]{.cite} [6 to 3]{.cite}

**Holding.** No. IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. The Court affirmed the Federal Circuit's judgment against the tariffs in the companion case and ordered the challenge brought in district court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

**Question.** Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes the President to impose tariffs, as he did in 2025 after declaring national emergencies over drug trafficking and trade deficits.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the opinion** (official text)

[Opinion: 607 U.S. ___](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1287_4gcj.pdf){.btn-official}
:::

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Learning Resources v. Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Learning_Resources,_Inc._v._Trump) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

The decision limits the [IEEPA](../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd) to its traditional tools, blocking and regulating transactions, and reaffirms that the taxing power, including tariffs, belongs to Congress unless it clearly delegates it. The sanctions programs built on IEEPA were not at issue. Tariffs now depend on statutes that expressly authorize them, such as [Section 232](../statutes/sec232-1962.qmd).

## How Congress responded

As of November 2026 Congress had not legislated on the question. The administration turned the same day to other tariff authorities, including Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974.

## Status

Good law; decided February 20, 2026.

## Statutes at issue

- [IEEPA](../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd){.subj}. Held that the act's authority to regulate importation does not include the power to impose tariffs.

Studied in [Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers](../study/units/emergencies-sanctions.qmd).
